review.summary: The paper presents a new dataset consisting of 7M videos with 234M video clips and their descriptions generated by language models. The paper also proposes a contrastive learning method for video-text representation learning, built upon a ViT-L backbone. The proposed method is evaluated on zero-shot action recognition and video retrieval tasks.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The paper does not provide enough evidence to demonstrate the advantage of the proposed dataset. Table 1 only shows that the size of the proposed dataset is larger than existing datasets. While in Table 2, 3, 4, the performance of the proposed method is worse than that of the model trained with WebVid10M, even with much more training data. For example, in Table 2, the model trained with WebVid10M achieves 59.88% accuracy on K400 in a zero-shot setting, while the model trained with the proposed dataset (named ViCLIP-200M) only achieves 59.7%. In Table 4, the model trained with WebVid10M achieves 42.4% on MSR-VTT in a zero-shot setting, while the model trained with the proposed dataset achieves 41.3%.

2. The paper argues that one of the advantages of the proposed dataset is that it contains more action-related words. However, the paper does not present any experiment to demonstrate that this is actually an advantage. In fact, as shown in Table 2, the model trained with the proposed dataset (DIV and FLT both) achieves worse zero-shot action recognition results on K700 than the model trained with WebVid10M.

3. The paper claims that the model trained with the proposed dataset can be used for text-to-video generation. However, the only provided experiment is a case study in the supplementary material, and no quantitative results are provided.

4. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the video caption quality. The paper only mentions that the captions are generated by language models, but does not provide any evaluation of the generated captions. For example, the paper does not provide any human evaluation results. Also, the paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the accuracy of the ASR transcripts.

review.summary: The authors present a novel approach to discover cell-type specific visual stimuli that can be used to classify neurons into functional cell types. They achieve this by alternately optimizing a clustering of neurons and the stimuli that best activates each cluster. They apply their method to 3 datasets across 2 species and 3 recording modalities and show that they recover known cell types.

weaknesses.issue:
I have some concerns about the novelty of the approach. Cell type classification algorithms have been extensively studied, and the approach seems very related to existing work, including the work of Baden et al. 2016 the authors cite. Moreover, the approach of alternately optimizing a clustering and the stimuli that best activates it is quite common. The authors should better clarify how their approach differs from existing work and what the novel contributions are. 

It is not clear how well the method generalizes to other cell types. The authors show that the method recovers known cell types, but it is not clear how well it will perform in the absence of known cell types. There are several approaches that do not require cell type labels to work. The authors should mention these approaches in the discussion, and ideally apply their method to a dataset without known cell types and compare the results to the unsupervised approaches.

# Review

## Summary
The authors present a novel approach to discover cell-type specific visual stimuli that can be used to classify neurons into functional cell types. They achieve this by alternately optimizing a clustering of neurons and the stimuli that best activates each cluster. They apply their method to 3 datasets across 2 species and 3 recording modalities and show that they recover known cell types.

## Soundness
4

## Presentation
4

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
The paper is well-written, and the algorithm is clearly explained. The authors apply their approach to three datasets from diverse systems and show that their method recovers known cell types. They also show that their method runs faster than an alternative cell typing approach. Thus, the method appears to work and provides an alternative to existing approaches.

## Weaknesses
I have some concerns about the novelty of the approach. Cell type classification algorithms have been extensively studied, and the approach seems very related to existing work, including the work of Baden et al. 2016 the authors cite. Moreover, the approach of alternately optimizing a clustering and the stimuli that best activates it is quite common. The authors should better clarify how their approach differs from existing work and what the novel contributions are. 

It is not clear how well the method generalizes to other cell types. The authors show that the method recovers known cell types, but it is not clear how well it will perform in the absence of known cell types. There are several approaches that do not require cell type labels to work. The authors should mention these approaches in the discussion, and ideally apply their method to a dataset without known cell types and compare the results to the unsupervised approaches.

## Questions
- There are several approaches that do not require cell type labels to perform cell type clustering, e.g., Chung et al., "Self-supervised identification of cell type-specific visual stimuli using neural network models", NeurIPS 2020. How does your approach compare to these methods?
- What happens if you apply your algorithm with no pre-trained digital twin and instead use a model that is trained online from the data? This would make the algorithm more useful in a variety of settings. 
- Are the cell type clusters you recover a subset of the original cell types, or do you recover some combinations of the original cell types? 
- How robust is the algorithm to poor predictions from the digital twin? Are there certain predictions that it is particularly bad at?
- What happens if you apply your algorithm with a larger number of initial clusters than cell types and then reduce the number of clusters? Does it tend to overestimate the number of cell types?

review.summary: The authors present a method for identifying cell types in visual systems by finding the most discriminative stimuli for different functional groups of neurons. This method relies on first training a model to predict neural responses to different stimuli (referred to as a "digital twin") and then using an EM-style algorithm to find clusters of neurons that respond similarly to specific stimuli. This method is validated in mouse retina, where cell types have been well-characterized, and is also used to find functional clusters in marmoset retina and macaque V4, where cell types have not been as extensively characterized. This method is faster than traditional techniques for identifying cell types and provides visual stimuli that can be used to identify cell types experimentally.

weaknesses.issue:
- The authors acknowledge that this method cannot capture motion, since the "digital twin" model they use cannot capture motion. Given the importance of direction selectivity in visual neurons, this is a major limitation of this method as it stands. One possible solution might be to use a "digital twin" model that can better capture motion, such as a transformer architecture. 
- As the authors acknowledge, the labels they have for the cell types in the mouse retina are not perfect. The authors do a good job of controlling for this in their analysis, but the noisiness of these labels is a potential source of variance in their results.

# Review

## Summary
The authors present a method for identifying cell types in visual systems by finding the most discriminative stimuli for different functional groups of neurons. This method relies on first training a model to predict neural responses to different stimuli (referred to as a "digital twin") and then using an EM-style algorithm to find clusters of neurons that respond similarly to specific stimuli. This method is validated in mouse retina, where cell types have been well-characterized, and is also used to find functional clusters in marmoset retina and macaque V4, where cell types have not been as extensively characterized. This method is faster than traditional techniques for identifying cell types and provides visual stimuli that can be used to identify cell types experimentally.

## Soundness
4

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
- This is a novel approach to identifying cell types that does not rely on pre-existing knowledge about cell types (besides the knowledge needed to train the "digital twin" model). The approach is also flexible, in that it can be applied to any brain area for which we have a "digital twin" model.
- The method is validated on mouse retina, where the cell types are known, and shows strong correspondence to known cell types.
- The method works in both gray-scale and color channels, and the authors demonstrate its use in both static and dynamic stimuli.
- The method is faster than traditional techniques for identifying cell types.

## Weaknesses
- The authors acknowledge that this method cannot capture motion, since the "digital twin" model they use cannot capture motion. Given the importance of direction selectivity in visual neurons, this is a major limitation of this method as it stands. One possible solution might be to use a "digital twin" model that can better capture motion, such as a transformer architecture. 
- As the authors acknowledge, the labels they have for the cell types in the mouse retina are not perfect. The authors do a good job of controlling for this in their analysis, but the noisiness of these labels is a potential source of variance in their results.

## Questions
- Is it possible to show that MDS can be used to identify cell types in an experiment? This is not strictly necessary given the existing validation, but would make a stronger case for this method.
- How robust is this method to noise in the "digital twin" model? Is there any analysis of how errors in the "digital twin" model propagate through the analysis? This is especially relevant for complex phenomena like direction selectivity, where errors may be amplified.

review.summary: The authors propose a method to find most discriminative stimuli (MDS) for functional cell types. Their algorithm alternates between (1) generating MDS for each cell type cluster, and (2) reassigning neurons to cell type clusters based on how well each MDS maximizes the neurons in the cluster while suppressing the activity of the neurons in other clusters. The authors validate the algorithm on mouse and marmoset retinal ganglion cells and macaque area V4.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The authors acknowledge that the mouse retinal ganglion cell results are not very impressive because the MDS method does not recover the same number of cell type clusters as the previous study by Baden et al. 2016. However, the authors do not provide a quantitative evaluation of how much worse the MDS method is compared to the method by Baden et al. 2016. In particular, how well do the recovered clusters predict the labels by Baden et al. 2016, and vice versa? This is important to evaluate the quality of the MDS approach compared to the previous approach by Baden et al. 2016.

2. The authors propose that their method is advantageous when there is little domain knowledge available about cell types. However, it is unclear how this method can work if there are no experimental measurements of neural responses available. In the experiments, the authors always first train a model to predict neural activity and then apply their algorithm to the predicted neural activity. If there are no experimental measurements of neural activity available, the authors' method would not work. In contrast, the previous method by Baden et al. 2016 does not require such models. How, then, is the proposed method advantageous if it requires experimental measurements of neural activity to train the predictive model?

# Review

## Summary
The authors propose a method to find most discriminative stimuli (MDS) for functional cell types. Their algorithm alternates between (1) generating MDS for each cell type cluster, and (2) reassigning neurons to cell type clusters based on how well each MDS maximizes the neurons in the cluster while suppressing the activity of the neurons in other clusters. The authors validate the algorithm on mouse and marmoset retinal ganglion cells and macaque area V4.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
The authors clearly describe the algorithm and present results on three datasets from different species and brain regions. They also compare their method to previous studies and discuss its advantages and disadvantages.

## Weaknesses
1. The authors acknowledge that the mouse retinal ganglion cell results are not very impressive because the MDS method does not recover the same number of cell type clusters as the previous study by Baden et al. 2016. However, the authors do not provide a quantitative evaluation of how much worse the MDS method is compared to the method by Baden et al. 2016. In particular, how well do the recovered clusters predict the labels by Baden et al. 2016, and vice versa? This is important to evaluate the quality of the MDS approach compared to the previous approach by Baden et al. 2016.

2. The authors propose that their method is advantageous when there is little domain knowledge available about cell types. However, it is unclear how this method can work if there are no experimental measurements of neural responses available. In the experiments, the authors always first train a model to predict neural activity and then apply their algorithm to the predicted neural activity. If there are no experimental measurements of neural activity available, the authors' method would not work. In contrast, the previous method by Baden et al. 2016 does not require such models. How, then, is the proposed method advantageous if it requires experimental measurements of neural activity to train the predictive model?

## Questions
1. In the caption of Figure 1, the authors state that the MEI approach by Bashivan et al. 2019 attempted to optimize images that both drive and suppress neurons, but that this is "often not possible in practice". Why is it not possible in practice? Could the authors please clarify?

2. In the first paragraph of the introduction, the authors state that "functional cell type identification currently often requires domain knowledge to hand-craft suitable visual fingerprinting stimuli". Could the authors please provide examples of "hand-craft suitable visual fingerprinting stimuli" and explain what is meant by "domain knowledge"?

3. At the end of the first paragraph of the introduction, the authors state that "each cell would 'see' a different part of the stimulus". I believe this statement is not necessarily true. For example, one could show full-field stimuli to a population of neurons while recording from them. In this case, all the neurons would see the full stimulus. Of course, the authors are correct that if one presents a spatially-varying stimulus, each neuron would see a different part of the stimulus.

4. In the second paragraph of the introduction, the authors state that "the neuron's preferred feature" can be identified by "optimizing images that do not only drive one neuron, but also suppress all others". I believe this statement is incorrect. The MEI approach optimizes stimuli that drive a particular neuron while suppressing other neurons, but it does not necessarily optimize for stimuli that only drive one neuron. In general, there is no reason to believe that a neuron's "preferred feature" can be identified with a single stimulus.

5. In the second paragraph of the introduction, the authors state that "multiple neurons of the same functional cell type are present". What is meant by "functional cell type"? This term is never defined. I believe the authors mean functional cell type cluster.

6. In the second paragraph of the introduction, the authors state that "multiple neurons of the same functional cell type are present, which respond similarly". What does "respond similarly" mean? What similarity is being referred to?

7. In the second paragraph of the introduction, the authors state that "With the resulting MDS, we can discover the unique visual features that the different cell types preferably process". How does the MDS approach "discover" unique visual features that different cell types prefer? What is the definition of "unique visual features"? How are these visual features discovered by the MDS approach?

8. At the end of the introduction, the authors state that their algorithm "extends this approach and find MDS at the cell type level". This statement is unclear. How does their algorithm extend the MEI approach? What does "find MDS at the cell type level" mean?

9. At the end of the introduction, the authors state that "As it is unknown which neurons belong to which cell type a priori, we need to cluster cells into types and find the MDS for each type in a joint procedure". The authors should explain why it is necessary to cluster cells into types if the goal is to find MDS for each type. It seems that one could find MDS for individual neurons without clustering them into types.

10. At the end of the introduction, the authors state that they "tackle this task in an EM-style manner". What is meant by "EM-style"? The authors should explain why they chose to use an EM-style approach and how their approach is similar to or different from the standard EM approach.

11. In the EM algorithm, why do the authors first optimize MDS and then reassign neurons to cell type clusters? It seems more standard to optimize the cluster assignments first and then the MDS. The authors should explain why they chose this non-standard ordering in the EM algorithm.

12. In Figure 1, the authors state that the MDS method can find "unique visual features". What is meant by "unique visual features"?

13. In Figure 1, the authors state that the MDS method can "discover the unique visual features that the different cell types preferably process". What is meant by "preferably process" in this context?

14. At the beginning of the results section, the authors state that "We empirically validate our novel clustering algorithm by benchmarking the resulting clusters against well-established RGC types". What is meant by "well-established RGC types"? Are these the same as "functional cell types"? The authors should explain these terms.

15. In the results section, the authors state that "we treated each cluster independently". What is meant by "treated each cluster independently"? Does this mean that each cluster is treated separately from all other clusters?

16. In the results section, the authors state that "the clusters we found comprised the well-known functional cluster hierarchy of the retina". What is meant by "the well-known functional cluster hierarchy of the retina"? The authors should explain this in more detail.

17. In the results section, the authors state that "the block-diagonal structure ... indicates that cell types were only confused within groups of very similar function". What does "block-diagonal structure" refer to? The authors should explain this in more detail.

18. In the results section, the authors state that "From the groups of Baden et al. 2016 types, fast ON types showed the clearest correspondence to a single MDS cluster". What is meant by "correspondence to a single MDS cluster"?

19. In the results section, the authors state that "In this group, one type even mapped exclusively to a single MDS cluster". What is meant by "mapped exclusively to a single MDS cluster"? Does this mean that all neurons in the type were assigned to the same MDS cluster?

20. In the results section, the authors state that "slow ON types were mapped to MDS clusters 5 and 6". Does this mean that neurons in the slow ON type were assigned to both MDS cluster 5 and MDS cluster 6?

21. In the results section, the authors state that "the biggest exception of the slow ON types was 'ON contrast suppressed', which did not map strongly to either cluster 5 or 6, but instead mapped to the color opponent MDS cluster 7". What is meant by "did not map strongly to either cluster 5 or 6"? What does it mean to "map strongly" to a cluster?

22. In the results section, the authors state that "this is expected, given that both types likely comprise sub-types with distinct functional properties". What is meant by "sub-types with distinct functional properties"?

23. In the results section, the authors state that "This is expected, given that both types likely comprise sub-types with distinct functional properties". This sentence seems to be repeated.

24. In the results section, the authors state that "To confirm this, we re-created cell type labels for a fairer comparison using a reduced classifier". What is meant by "re-created cell type labels"?

25. In the results section, the authors state that "This indicates that without access to direction selectivity or morphological features (e.g. soma size) the finer Baden et al. 2016 types cannot be reliably distinguished". Why can't these types be reliably distinguished? The authors should explain this in more detail.

26. In the results section, the authors state that "This also explains why our MDS clustering finds fewer clusters". How does the fact that MDS clustering finds fewer clusters explain why the Baden et al. 2016 types cannot be reliably distinguished?

27. In the results section, the authors state that "The similarity of clusters across nine comparison runs was also high (median ARI: 0.96)". What is an ARI?

28. In the results section, the authors state that "Although the number of cells is smaller and the taxonomy of functional types is less refined for the marmoset retina, the results on this dataset show that MDS clustering finds meaningful clusters across species and recording techniques". How do the results show that MDS clustering finds meaningful clusters? What is meant by "meaningful clusters"?

29. In the results section, the authors state that "Finally, we showed that our approach extends beyond the retina and also works for brain areas with little domain knowledge about cell types". How does the approach "extend beyond the retina"? In what way does the approach work for brain areas with little domain knowledge about cell types? The authors should explain this in more detail.

30. In the results section, the authors state that "Here, the MDS were individual images, which showed complex patterns with curvature or texture, typical for V4". What is meant by "complex patterns with curvature or texture"? The authors should explain this in more detail.

review.summary: This paper proposes the LASER technique: a method that improves the reasoning abilities of LLMs by reducing the rank of specific weight matrices in specific layers of a Transformer model. The technique is the following: one identifies the weight matrix for which reducing its rank results in the largest performance increase, then this matrix is replaced with its rank-$k$ approximation (for some $k$ fraction of the original rank). The authors demonstrate that this technique can improve the reasoning abilities of several LLMs on several reasoning tasks (e.g., HotPotQA, FEVER, CounterFact, etc.), and also demonstrate that LASER improves the performance of a decision Transformer on the Sokoban game.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The motivation behind the technique is not clear. The authors state that “we find that these reductions can produce drastic improvements in accuracy”, but it is not clear why this is the case. The authors present some analysis and hypotheses (e.g., that higher-order components of some of these matrices encode either high-frequency words or alternate answers of the same semantic type as the correct answer), but I found it hard to understand why this is the case.
2. The technique seems to be specific to reasoning tasks. The authors state that “we find that the largest improvements in the model accuracy correspond to information that is less common in the training data”, which is consistent with the fact that the proposed technique improves the performance on QA datasets. But what about tasks that are not QA? What about, for example, tasks that require more general language generation? The authors do not show any results on such tasks. Moreover, the technique does not seem to improve performance on the Epistemic Reasoning task (but only hurts it). This leads me to believe that the technique is specific to QA tasks, and is not a general technique for improving the reasoning abilities of LLMs.
3. The technique requires some hyper-parameter tuning. The authors state that “the search is done on a validation set, and results are reported on the test set”. I am not sure if this is a fair evaluation, as the hyper-parameters were tuned for the test set. I would recommend that the authors use a separate set of validation data (e.g., a subset of the training data), and tune the hyper-parameters only on this set (and not on the test set).
4. The technique does not improve the performance of Llama2 on 5 out of the 6 tasks presented in Table 1. Specifically, the authors show that LASER hurts performance on the Epistemic Reasoning task. Moreover, the improvement on the remaining tasks is relatively small. Overall, this hurts the significance of the method. The authors should present results on more models. Specifically, I would recommend that the authors present results on larger models (e.g., Llama 70B, Llama 405B, etc.), as these models have been shown to achieve better performance on reasoning tasks. I would also recommend that the authors show results on the GPT-4 model, as this is one of the strongest models out there.

This paper proposes a new method for imitation learning based on the recently proposed forward-backward (FB) framework. The FB framework learns a set of parametrized policies $\pi_z$ and a state feature $B(s)$ such that the successor measure of a policy $\pi_z$ can be expressed as the integral of $B(s)$ against $\pi_z$.
In imitation learning, the FB model is trained on a dataset of expert trajectories and used to extract a policy $\pi_z$ corresponding to a desired reward function or imitation objective, and this policy is then refined with either a gradient-based optimization or a forward pass. This approach is shown to be effective across a variety of imitation learning principles, including behavioral cloning, reward-based imitation, distribution/apprenticeship learning and goal-based imitation. The authors show that the proposed method performs comparably or better than a number of offline RL imitation learning baselines, and is significantly faster than the baselines.

weaknesses.issue:

- The experiments are run in relatively low-dimensional environments. It would be interesting to see how the method performs on more complex tasks, such as humanoid.

# Review

## Summary
This paper proposes a new method for imitation learning based on the recently proposed forward-backward (FB) framework. The FB framework learns a set of parametrized policies $\pi_z$ and a state feature $B(s)$ such that the successor measure of a policy $\pi_z$ can be expressed as the integral of $B(s)$ against $\pi_z$.
In imitation learning, the FB model is trained on a dataset of expert trajectories and used to extract a policy $\pi_z$ corresponding to a desired reward function or imitation objective, and this policy is then refined with either a gradient-based optimization or a forward pass. This approach is shown to be effective across a variety of imitation learning principles, including behavioral cloning, reward-based imitation, distribution/apprenticeship learning and goal-based imitation. The authors show that the proposed method performs comparably or better than a number of offline RL imitation learning baselines, and is significantly faster than the baselines.

## Soundness
4

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
This is a strong paper overall. The method is presented very clearly, and the claims are well supported. The FB framework is a natural approach to imitation learning, and the experiments show that it performs well across the board relative to a variety of baselines.

## Weaknesses
- I found some of the discussion around goal-based imitation a bit difficult to follow. I think the section could be improved with a diagram illustrating how the method works. 
- The experiments are run with only a single expert trajectory. While this is understandable given that many imitation learning settings work with a small number of demonstrations, it would be good to see how the method performs with more expert trajectories, as this is more in line with typical offline RL settings. 
- The experiments are run in relatively low-dimensional environments. It would be interesting to see how the method performs on more complex tasks, such as humanoid.

## Questions
- In section 4.3, the authors discuss various approaches to distribution matching and feature matching within the FB framework. However, the losses presented in equations 12, 13, 14 all seem to be for distribution matching, not feature matching. Feature matching would minimize the distance between $\rho_e$ and $\rho_\pi$, whereas equations 12, 13, 14 minimize the distance between $M^{\pi_e}$ and $M^{\pi_z}$. I'm not sure what is meant by the distinction between feature matching and distribution matching in this context. 
- In section 5.1, the authors state that the baselines were implemented using the same unsupervised dataset as the FB model. However, in section 5.2, the authors state that the BFM methods reported in Figure 3 use a different pre-trained FB model. Which is the case? 
- In section 5.1, the authors state that the FB model is "effectively learning to predict the next state given a state and an action". This is not quite right, since the FB model does not take actions as input. The successor measure $M^{\pi_z}$ induced by a policy $\pi_z$ does give a prediction of the next state distribution, but the FB model itself does not. This statement could be rephrased to avoid this confusion. 
- I was curious whether the authors have considered using the FB approach for online imitation learning. In this setting, one could use the FB model to extract a policy $\pi_z$ from the expert's current state and then use this policy to take an action. This would allow the policy to improve over time. 
- In section 4.4, the authors state that the expert policy cannot be recovered by a stationary policy. I don't think this is quite right. The expert policy can certainly be recovered by a stationary policy, but it may not be learnable by a stationary policy due to distributional shift. 
- The proposed method seems to be related to optimal transport, particularly the reward-based imitation learning and distribution matching objectives. I was curious whether the authors have considered making the connection to optimal transport literature explicitly.

review.summary: The paper explores imitation learning (IL) through the lens of the forward-backward (FB) framework, a recent RL approach based on successor measures. The FB framework learns a tractable representation of successor measures to approximate optimal policies for any reward, which is useful for IL. The authors leverage FB to derive several IL algorithms: behavioral cloning, reward-based IL, distribution matching, and goal-based imitation. The authors evaluate these algorithms in four simulated environments, showing that FB-IL methods perform at least as well as state-of-the-art offline IL algorithms while requiring significantly less time to generate an imitation policy from a few expert demonstrations.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The main weakness of the paper is the lack of novelty, as it is a straightforward application of the FB framework to IL. The authors do not provide significant theoretical contributions beyond the work of Touati & Ollivier (2021). The paper's theoretical contributions are limited to reiterating the FB framework and stating that the proposed IL methods are consistent with FB principles, without providing new theoretical guarantees or insights.
2. The experimental evaluation is limited to four simulated environments, which is not sufficient to demonstrate the generality of the proposed approach. The authors should evaluate their methods in more complex environments, such as humanoid, to show that FB-IL can be applied to more challenging tasks.
3. The paper claims that FB-IL methods perform at least as well as state-of-the-art offline IL algorithms, but this is not true for all tasks and baselines. For example, in the Cheetah environment, the proposed methods perform significantly worse than the offline RL baseline OTR. The paper should provide a more detailed analysis of the results, including a discussion of the tasks where FB-IL methods underperform and potential reasons for this.
4. The paper should provide a more detailed analysis of the pre-training phase, including the amount of data required for FB to learn an effective representation of successor measures.

* I don't understand why the proposed model is called a "latent diffusion model", it doesn't seem to use any diffusion process.
* The P-LLM model is not described at all, can you explain it in more detail?
* In section 3.1, it is assumed that the mutual information between y_t and \tilde{y} only contains timbre information, can you explain this in more detail?
* In section 3.1, the author state that "if we only feed phoneme sequence to E_c, E_c can only pass all the content information z_c". I assume that z_c is the output of the content encoder, which is fed into the cross attention along with the embeddings of the reference audio. But how does the model know which are the reference frames and which is the target frame, if all of them are concatenated together?
* In section 3.2, the authors state that the VQ encoder "captures the correlation of features", can you explain how this is done?
* In section 3.2, the authors state that the timbre encoder "extracts fine-grained timbre information from multiple prompts that can represent the speakers' habits". But the reference audio is concatenated, so how can it extract different habits?
* In section 3.2 the authors state that the model upsamples the output of the timbre-to-content attention module to match the length of the target mel-spectrogram. But how does the model know the length of the target mel-spectrogram, at this point the target mel-spectrogram has not been generated yet.
* In section 3.3 the authors state that z_c is expanded to the frame level with duration information, but z_c is the output of the content encoder, which is a scalar, so how is this expansion done?
* In section 3.3 the authors state that "we transform u' to prosody code". How is this done?
* I don't understand how the interpolation is done, can you explain it in more detail?
* I don't understand how the RTF is calculated, can you explain?
* The results in table 1 are not very convincing, the difference between 60s and 300s is quite small. I think it would be interesting to see how long the model can go, maybe with 900s or 1min of reference audio.
* I think it would be interesting to compare with NaturalSpeech 2, which is zero-shot and able to utilise long reference audio.

review.summary:
The paper presents a new dataset for reasoning with LLMs. The dataset is generated with the following process:

1. Create a set of core facts required to solve a problem (e.g. "John is the killer" and "John had a motive" in the case of a murder mystery)
2. Create a reasoning tree by recursively expanding facts with an LLM
3. Create a story by expanding the leaves of the tree with an LLM

The authors then evaluate a number of LLMs on the dataset and show that they are still struggling on this type of problems.

weaknesses.issue:
The dataset creation algorithm is a straightforward extension of existing datasets like True Detective (which is mentioned in the paper). The three domains (Murder Mystery, Object Placement, and Team Allocation) are also already well covered by existing datasets. I can't see how this new dataset is adding significantly to the existing evaluation options for LLMs.

The authors argue that their synthetic dataset is better than existing datasets because it can be updated as LLMs improve. This argument has some merit, however I think it is slightly overstated. If LLMs can solve the tasks in this dataset, then it will become trivial to generate new, more complex instances of the tasks. And if LLMs can't solve the tasks, then it won't matter that the dataset can be updated as the LLMs won't be able to solve the new instances.

The authors argue that their dataset is more natural than existing datasets like bAbI or BigTOM. However, a quick look at some of the examples in the Appendix shows that the stories are not very coherent and contain a lot of repeated text. I think the authors should have considered using a more recent LLM for story generation, instead of sticking with GPT-4.

# Review

## Summary
The paper presents a new dataset for reasoning with LLMs. The dataset is generated with the following process:

1. Create a set of core facts required to solve a problem (e.g. "John is the killer" and "John had a motive" in the case of a murder mystery)
2. Create a reasoning tree by recursively expanding facts with an LLM
3. Create a story by expanding the leaves of the tree with an LLM

The authors then evaluate a number of LLMs on the dataset and show that they are still struggling on this type of problems.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
The paper is well written and easy to follow. The authors present a nice summary of existing datasets in Table 1. The dataset generation procedure seems sound and is well explained. The experiments are well done and presented.

## Weaknesses
The dataset creation algorithm is a straightforward extension of existing datasets like True Detective (which is mentioned in the paper). The three domains (Murder Mystery, Object Placement, and Team Allocation) are also already well covered by existing datasets. I can't see how this new dataset is adding significantly to the existing evaluation options for LLMs.

The authors argue that their synthetic dataset is better than existing datasets because it can be updated as LLMs improve. This argument has some merit, however I think it is slightly overstated. If LLMs can solve the tasks in this dataset, then it will become trivial to generate new, more complex instances of the tasks. And if LLMs can't solve the tasks, then it won't matter that the dataset can be updated as the LLMs won't be able to solve the new instances.

The authors argue that their dataset is more natural than existing datasets like bAbI or BigTOM. However, a quick look at some of the examples in the Appendix shows that the stories are not very coherent and contain a lot of repeated text. I think the authors should have considered using a more recent LLM for story generation, instead of sticking with GPT-4.

## Questions
I'm not sure what the "commonsense" aspect of the dataset is referring to. Is it just the fact that the stories are written in natural language instead of a formal representation?

I don't see how "Not solvable w/rules" is a pro. In general, I would think that if a problem can be solved with rules, then that is a good thing. Are the authors arguing that we want to create problems that cannot be solved with rules because...?

In the "Ablating our creation process" section, how did you evaluate GPT-4's performance? Did you use the same zero-shot, few-shot, etc. evaluation as the models in Table 2?

review.summary: In this paper, the authors focus on the link prediction task and propose a new architecture called MPNN-then-SF, which runs the MPNN first and then uses structural features to guide the pooling of node representations. To further address the issue of graph incompleteness, the authors also introduce a common neighbor completion strategy. Experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The contribution is limited. The proposed model is incremental based on existing works and the used techniques are also quite common in the literature, like the MPNN-and-SF models.

2. The authors argue that the MPNN-then-SF is better than the MPNN-and-SF models because it can capture node properties of common neighbors. But I am confused about this point. In my opinion, the common neighbors are just nodes, why the properties of common neighbors are so important? Why not the properties of the target nodes themselves are more important?

3. The authors argue that the MPNN-then-SF is better than the SF-then-MPNN models because it runs the MPNN only once for all target links. However, I think this is not a big issue since the complexity of the link prediction task is O(N^2) anyway, whether we run the MPNN once or N times.

4. I think the issue of graph incompleteness has been well studied in previous works. The authors should discuss more about the differences between the proposed method with them.

5. The presentation of the paper can be improved. For example, the authors should clearly define the term "expressivity". What does the symbol "|"| mean?

6. The authors only consider the first-order neighbors in the NCN model, but the high-order neighbors are more important in the literature. Why not consider the high-order neighbors in the NCN model?

7. The authors should conduct experiments to validate the effectiveness of the proposed common neighbor completion strategy.

review.summary: This paper introduces a diffusion-based method for dense matching, named DiffMatch. The proposed method aims to estimate the optimal matching field by modeling the matching field distribution within the diffusion process. To this end, DiffMatch leverages the conditional denoising diffusion model, which takes the matching cost and the initial flow as input. The authors further propose a flow upsampling diffusion model to enhance the resolution of the matching field. Experiments are conducted on standard datasets and the proposed method achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The motivation of the proposed method is not clear. In the abstract, the authors claim that recent approaches have focused on learning the data term with deep neural networks without explicitly modeling the prior. However, in their method section, they do not point out what is the prior term. In Section 2, the authors claim that they aim to learn the posterior distribution of dense correspondence, which is in fact the matching probability distribution conditioned on the feature descriptors, and is the data term in the probabilistic interpretation of dense correspondence. Thus, it is confusing what is the prior term and what is the data term in the proposed method.
2. The proposed method is not well formulated. As mentioned above, the matching probability distribution conditioned on the feature descriptors (i.e., the data term) is the optimal solution to the dense matching problem. However, the authors aim to learn such a distribution through a diffusion process, which is confusing. In addition, it is not clear why a diffusion process is able to learn the matching prior.
3. The proposed method introduces a cascaded diffusion model to enhance the resolution of the matching field. However, no ablation study is provided to verify the effectiveness of the cascaded diffusion model.

review.summary: This paper studies the problem of learning neural implicit representations (NIR) for video sequences. In contrast to existing methods that learn a single representation for a given dataset, this paper studies a more realistic setting where multiple video sequences are learned incrementally, with a goal of learning a robust representation for each video sequence while maintaining good quality for previous sequences. To this end, the authors propose a new method, the Progressive Fourier Neural Representation (PFNR), which learns to sparsify the representation by learning a binary mask for each sequence in the Fourier domain. The authors demonstrate that PFNR outperforms a number of continual learning baselines in the UVG dataset.

review.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of spatio-temporal modeling for smart city applications, particularly in data-scarce cities. The authors propose a novel generative pre-training framework called GPD for spatio-temporal few-shot learning with urban knowledge transfer. This approach recasts spatio-temporal few-shot learning as pre-training a generative diffusion model that generates tailored neural networks guided by prompts. The GPD framework employs a Transformer-based diffusion model and city-specific prompts to generate adaptive parameters for cities, allowing for adaptability to diverse data distributions. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of GPD on multiple real-world datasets for tasks such as traffic speed prediction and crowd flow prediction, showing consistent outperformance over state-of-the-art baselines.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The construction of spatio-temporal graphs is usually costly, especially for large-scale cities. This process involves collecting and integrating various data sources, which requires significant computational resources and time. Additionally, the quality of the graphs heavily relies on the accuracy and timeliness of the data, which can be affected by factors such as data collection policies, the presence of noise, and the accuracy of geocoding and spatial referencing.
2. This paper does not include sufficient experiments to demonstrate the scalability of GPD, especially in very large-scale cities. The experiments are conducted on datasets from cities like New York City, Washington, D.C., and Baltimore, which are relatively smaller in terms of population and geographical size. To fully evaluate the scalability of GPD, it is recommended to test the framework on larger cities such as London, Tokyo, or New York City (the entire city). These cities offer more extensive datasets and more complex urban environments, which can help to better assess the performance and scalability of GPD.
3. In the prompt section, only node embeddings extracted from a pre-trained knowledge graph are used as spatial prompts. It is recommended to include more static features, such as population, region area, functional type, and the distribution of points of interest (POI), as suggested in the paper.
4. The experiments conducted in the paper do not adequately demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed method. Specifically, there is a lack of comparison between the proposed method and other baseline approaches in terms of computational efficiency and resource utilization. Additionally, the paper does not provide detailed information about the computational resources required for the experiments, such as the type and number of GPUs used, as well as the running time and memory consumption of the proposed method and baseline approaches. 
5. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the limitations of the proposed method. This omission can limit the understanding of the applicability and potential constraints of GPD in real-world scenarios. It is recommended to include a section discussing the limitations of the proposed method, such as the sensitivity to the quality of the spatio-temporal graphs, the computational efficiency, and the potential biases introduced by the prompts.

review.summary: This paper proposes a new method to reconstruct 3D objects from a small number of unposed images. The method uses a transformer to predict both the pose and shape (in the form of a NeRF) from unposed images. The transformer is trained using large datasets of posed images from Objaverse and MVImgNet. During training, the NeRF tokens and image tokens are passed to the transformer, and the NeRF tokens are supervised with a rendering loss. For pose estimation, the image tokens are used to predict 3D points in space, which are then used in a differentiable PnP solver to estimate the pose. During inference, the method predicts the NeRF and pose for a set of unposed images. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms a number of prior works on a number of datasets.

weaknesses.issue:
- The method assumes that the camera intrinsics are known. I think it should be possible to extend the method to predict the intrinsics as well.
- The method only predicts a low resolution NeRF. High resolution reconstruction of the NeRF is an active area of research, and is not directly related to the pose estimation problem, but it would be nice to have higher resolution reconstructions.
- The method cannot handle significant pose variations. For example, the method is not able to handle a phone lying flat on a table, where the camera looking down on it from the top. The input images would be very different from the training images, and the method would not work. The method seems to work best when the input images are within the distribution of the training images.
- The method is very large, and requires a lot of computation and memory to train and test.

## Summary
This paper proposes a new method to reconstruct 3D objects from a small number of unposed images. The method uses a transformer to predict both the pose and shape (in the form of a NeRF) from unposed images. The transformer is trained using large datasets of posed images from Objaverse and MVImgNet. During training, the NeRF tokens and image tokens are passed to the transformer, and the NeRF tokens are supervised with a rendering loss. For pose estimation, the image tokens are used to predict 3D points in space, which are then used in a differentiable PnP solver to estimate the pose. During inference, the method predicts the NeRF and pose for a set of unposed images. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms a number of prior works on a number of datasets.

## Soundness
4

## Presentation
4

## Contribution
4

## Strengths
- The proposed method is quite simple and elegant. It is based on a straightforward transformer architecture. The fact that the method can predict the pose and NeRF simultaneously is quite clever, and allows for a unified training and inference pipeline.
- The results are very good. The method is able to reconstruct the shape and estimate the camera pose from as few as 2 images (though it is not shown any results with only 2 views in the paper).
- The proposed method can generalize to unseen datasets.

## Weaknesses
- The method assumes that the camera intrinsics are known. I think it should be possible to extend the method to predict the intrinsics as well.
- The method only predicts a low resolution NeRF. High resolution reconstruction of the NeRF is an active area of research, and is not directly related to the pose estimation problem, but it would be nice to have higher resolution reconstructions.
- The method cannot handle significant pose variations. For example, the method is not able to handle a phone lying flat on a table, where the camera looking down on it from the top. The input images would be very different from the training images, and the method would not work. The method seems to work best when the input images are within the distribution of the training images.
- The method is very large, and requires a lot of computation and memory to train and test.

## Questions
- The method assumes that the camera intrinsics are known. Is it possible to extend the method to predict the intrinsics as well? This would allow the method to be even more general.
- What is the effect of noise in the input images? All of the experiments assume that the input images are of very high quality. It would be good to show how the method performs when there is noise in the input images.
- How does the method perform with more input views? All of the experiments use 4 input views, but it would be interesting to see how the method performs with 2 or 3 input views. This would give more insight into the minimum number of views required for the method to work.
- In Fig. 2, what do the input and output poses look like? It would be helpful to see how the estimated pose compares to the input pose.

review.summary: This paper presents an empirical study on the target representation for masked image modeling (MIM) pre-training. The key finding is that the choice of the target representation is less critical for learning good visual representation. Based on this observation, this paper further proposes a multi-stage MIM training method with a randomly initialized model as the teacher. The proposed method is evaluated on various downstream tasks, including classification, transfer learning, object detection, and semantic segmentation.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The novelty of this paper is somewhat limited. The key finding that the choice of the target representation is less critical for learning good visual representation has been discussed in previous works. For example, MAE [1] has shown that using random noise as the target can achieve comparable performance with using the original image as the target. data2vec [2] has shown that using the mean of the features from different augmentations as the target can achieve comparable performance with using the CLIP [3] representation as the target. This paper does not present new insights into the role of the target representation in MIM. The proposed method of using a randomly initialized model as the teacher is also straightforward.

2. The paper does not discuss the difference between the proposed method and data2vec. Data2vec also uses randomly initialized models as the teacher and updates the teacher based on the student. The key difference is that this paper uses a multi-stage distillation pipeline, while data2vec uses a single stage. However, the advantage of the multi-stage distillation pipeline is not clear. In fact, as shown in Table 8, using a single stage with 1600 epochs can achieve comparable performance with using two stages.

3. The paper does not compare the proposed method with data2vec. As mentioned in point 2, the proposed method is very similar to data2vec. It is important to compare the proposed method with data2vec to understand the difference in performance and efficiency.


[1] He, Kaiming, et al. "Masked autoencoders are scalable vision learners." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2022.

[2] Baevski, Alexei, et al. "data2vec: A general framework for self-supervised learning in speech, vision and language." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2022.

[3] Radford, Alec, et al. "Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision." International conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2021.

review.summary: This paper studies the influence of target representations in masked image modeling (MIM). By comparing four different MIM paradigms, the authors conclude that a carefully design of the target is unnecessary for learning good visual representations. They further propose a multi-stage MIM pipeline that repeatedly change the student to teacher and continue the training, which achieves better performance than previous methods.

weaknesses.issue:
1. My major concern is the novelty of this paper. The main conclusion that different target representations derive similarly behaved models, and the proposed multi-stage training pipeline have already been discussed in iBOT. The main difference of this paper is the multi-stage training paradigm, which seems incremental to me.

2. The authors emphasize that they use a randomly initialized model as the teacher, while in fact, the random teacher is just a masked image modeling with pixel as the target. Therefore, I think the proposed method can also be regarded as a kind of MIM with pixel as the target, which makes the difference between this paper and previous methods less significant. 

3. The authors claim that the proposed method can avoid the extra pre-training stage, while in fact, the training cost is even larger since the model needs to be trained for multiple stages.

review.summary: The paper first shows that the target representation is unnecessary for learning good visual representation since different targets tend to derive similarly behaved models. Then, it proposes a multi-stage masked distillation pipeline and uses a randomly initialized model as the teacher, enabling it to effectively train high-capacity models without any effort to carefully design the target representation. Experiments on various downstream tasks of classification, transfer learning, object detection, and semantic segmentation show that the proposed method outperforms previous self-supervised methods by nontrivial margins.

weaknesses.issue:
- The novelty of the paper is somewhat limited. The major difference from the existing masked image modeling methods is that the proposed method uses a randomly initialized model as the teacher model and updates it in multiple stages. However, the idea of updating the teacher model in multiple stages is similar to iBOT and data2vec. The difference is that the proposed method uses a randomly initialized model as the teacher while IBOT and data2vec use the EMA of the student model as the teacher. Moreover, the finding that the target representation is not necessary has been shown in MAE. 
- The finding that the choice of the teacher model does not significantly affect the performance of masked image modeling is somewhat counterintuitive. In the proposed method, the student model is updated towards the randomly initialized teacher model in the first stage. The randomly initialized teacher model does not provide any meaningful information about the masked data. It is unclear why updating the randomly initialized model can still give good performance.

review.summary: The paper introduces the problem of label transfer in object detection to address annotation mismatches across different datasets. The authors propose a data-centric approach called Label-Guided Pseudo-Labeling (LGPL) that improves downstream object detection performance by transferring bounding boxes from source datasets to match the annotation style of a target dataset. The paper validates the effectiveness of LGPL in four object detection scenarios defined over seven different datasets and three different architectures, showing an average improvement of 1.88 mAP and 2.65 AP^75. The paper also demonstrates that addressing annotation mismatches with LGPL can improve object detection better than off-the-shelf supervised domain adaptation techniques that align instance features.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The paper does not provide sufficient information on the computational efficiency and scalability of the proposed LGPL approach, which could be a concern for large-scale applications.
2. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the impact of different factors, such as the size of the source dataset, the complexity of the annotation protocol, and the number of classes, on the performance of the label transfer model.
3. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the interpretability of the label transfer model and how it handles ambiguous or challenging cases.
4. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the robustness of the label transfer model to different types of data corruption or perturbations.

The main idea is to augment the training objectives with a contrastive loss term that aligns the intermediate layer outputs with static or adaptive label embeddings. The proposed method, Difficulty-Aware Task Sampler (DATS), aims to allocate training effort to task samples in proportion to their difficulty, thereby minimizing validation error across a discrete set of tasks. The authors present two strategies to implement DATS: adaptive weighting of training loss and adaptive allocation of residual points. Through experiments with DATS, they demonstrate improved performance in meta-learning, particularly in reducing the disparity between best and worst-performing models.

## Soundness
3

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
2

## Strengths
The paper introduces a novel approach to task sampling in the meta-training of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). The idea of allocating training effort in proportion to task difficulty is both creative and logical, addressing a gap in the existing literature. The clarity of the manuscript is commendable, with a well-structured presentation of the proposed method and clear explanations of the experimental setup and results. The significance of the work is evident in its potential impact on the field of machine learning for scientific computing, particularly in improving the efficiency and effectiveness of meta-learning approaches for PINNs. Overall, the originality, quality, and clarity of the paper make it a valuable contribution to the field.

## Weaknesses
While the proposed method is innovative, its practical application may be challenging due to the need to determine the difficulty of each task, which can be a complex task in itself. The manuscript does not provide a clear and generalizable method for assessing task difficulty, which may limit its broad applicability. Additionally, the experiments conducted are limited in scope, focusing primarily on the Burgers' equation, which may not fully represent the behavior of the proposed method across a wider range of PDEs and problem domains. The paper would benefit from a more diverse set of experiments to validate the generalizability of the proposed approach. Lastly, while the manuscript is generally clear, it could benefit from further clarification on certain aspects, such as the specific definition of residual points and the relationship between training and validation sets. 2. The experimental results are not convincing. The proposed method is only evaluated on the classification task. However, TaskArithmetics and Ties-Merging can handle different tasks, including classification, regression, and even dense prediction. Besides, the proposed method is only evaluated on 8 tasks, which is much less than the 16 tasks in TaskArithmetics and Ties-Merging. ## Summary
The paper presents AdaMerging, a novel approach for multi-task learning that improves model merging without requiring original training data. Traditional task vector-based methods in multi-task learning (MTL) have shown promising results but are sensitive to merging coefficients, leading to performance issues. AdaMering addresses this by autonomously learning task-specific or layer-specific coefficients through entropy minimization on unlabeled test data. The method significantly enhances performance, generalization, and robustness across various tasks and data distributions, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods.

## Soundness
2

## Presentation
3

## Contribution
3

## Strengths
1. This paper introduces a novel approach to multi-task learning by addressing the challenge of model merging without relying on original training data, which is a significant step forward in the field. The method's ability to autonomously learn merging coefficients through entropy minimization on unlabeled test samples is innovative and effective.

2. The paper is well-written and easy to understand. The authors provide clear explanations of the proposed method and its advantages.

3. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of AdaMerging through extensive experiments across multiple tasks and datasets. The results show substantial improvements in accuracy, generalization to unseen tasks, and robustness to data distribution shifts, highlighting the method's practical applicability and robustness.

## Weaknesses
1. The paper lacks a detailed analysis of the computational complexity and scalability of the proposed method. It would be beneficial to discuss the computational requirements and how the method scales with an increasing number of tasks and model size.

2. The paper does not provide a thorough discussion on the interpretability of the learned merging coefficients. Understanding why certain coefficients are assigned to specific tasks or layers can provide additional insights and improve trust in the method.

3. The proposed method relies on entropy minimization on unlabeled test samples. A more detailed analysis of the method's sensitivity to the quality and distribution of these unlabeled samples would be beneficial.

2. Can the authors provide more insights into how the learned merging coefficients relate to the specific characteristics of each task, and whether there are patterns or correlations?

3. How does the choice of unlabeled test samples for entropy minimization affect the performance of AdaMerging, and how sensitive is the method to the quality and distribution of these samples?

review.summary: This paper proposes an adaptive merging method for the task arithmetic of multi-task learning. Based on the observation that the performance of task arithmetic is very sensitive to the parameter $\lambda$, which controls the strength of the task vector, this paper proposes to use the model's prediction entropy on the test set as a surrogate objective to optimize $\lambda$. The proposed method is validated on eight classification tasks and shows improved performance over previous task arithmetic methods.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The proposed method is not well-motivated. The authors claim that the model's prediction entropy can serve as a proxy of the loss, but this correlation does not mean that the model's prediction entropy can be directly used to optimize the loss. Moreover, the authors do not explain why we should optimize the prediction entropy, which is also not related to the performance of model merging. 
2. The proposed method requires testing data for optimization, but previous task arithmetic methods do not require testing data. Therefore, the comparison in Figure 3 is unfair, as other methods do not use the testing data. 
3. The proposed method may have a high risk of overfitting, as the model will be optimized on the testing set.
4. In Table 1, the proposed method is inferior to the traditional multi-task learning method on the ViT-B/32 model, which does not show the advantage of the proposed method.

review.summary: This paper studies how well large language models (LLMs) can capture the distribution of possible meanings of ambiguous inputs. The authors introduce a new dataset and framework called AmP to address the shortcomings of existing tasks that map language to formal representations, which often ignore or remove ambiguity. The authors define templates to generate data for five well-documented linguistic ambiguities and investigate how several few-shot text-to-code systems handle ambiguity. They propose three new metrics to measure the extent to which models capture ambiguity and provide a framework for improving their ability to predict multiple meanings. The paper finds that while LLMs struggle to capture the distribution of possible meanings without explicit instruction, they are able to capture it well when ambiguity is attested in their inputs.

weaknesses.issue:
The paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion of the limitations of the proposed metrics and framework. It would be helpful to provide examples of cases where the metrics fail to capture the ambiguity or where the framework fails to provide meaningful insights. 

The paper could also benefit from a more detailed analysis of the impact of different factors on the performance of LLMs on ambiguity. For example, it would be interesting to investigate how the performance of LLMs on ambiguity varies with the complexity of the input sentence, the frequency of the ambiguity in the training data, or the specific architecture used by the LLM.

This paper proposes a new method for graph metric learning based on maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). review.summary: The paper proposes a manifold preserving guided diffusion method, which leverages pretrained diffusion models and off-the-shelf neural networks for a broad range of tasks without extra training. The method is based on the manifold hypothesis, which assumes that real data lies on a manifold. The authors propose to project the guidance to the manifold using its tangent spaces throughout the diffusion process. They also introduce a shortcut for guidance gradients using DDIM sampling, which improves sample quality and efficiency. The method is evaluated on various conditional generation tasks such as solving noisy linear inverse problems, FaceID guidance, and text-to-image generation.

The authors provide a theoretical framework for understanding ESC, and they propose an optimization strategy for selecting the window size and maximum sampling times. weaknesses.issue:
- The experimental results are not entirely convincing:
    - The performance improvement of ESC over SC is marginal, with the largest gain being only 0.3% (Table 1). This raises questions about the practical significance of ESC.
    - The reported performance of the baseline SC method is lower than expected. For instance, SC-GPT4 achieves only 60.32% accuracy on MATH, while the official GPT-4 API reports 69.12% accuracy (https://platform.openai.com/docs/models/gpt-4). This discrepancy suggests that the baseline may not have been adequately tuned.
    - The performance of ESC appears to be sensitive to the window size. In Table 2, ESC shows a -2.44% decrease in performance when the window size increases from 8 to 16. This sensitivity raises concerns about the generalizability of ESC.
- The paper lacks a comparison with other efficient variants of self-consistency, such as the one proposed by [1].
- The paper contains several grammatical errors and typos. For example, in Section 1, the phrase should be "based on this" instead of "based on this." In Section 2, "citet" should be used instead of "citep." A thorough proofreading is recommended to enhance the readability.

[1] Yao, Shunyu, et al. "Efficient self-consistency decoding by dynamic early stopping." arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.00600 (2023).

- The optimization strategy for ESC shows promise in achieving an optimal balance between performance and cost, and the results are supported by theoretical analysis.

## Weaknesses
- The experimental results are not entirely convincing:
    - The performance improvement of ESC over SC is marginal, with the largest gain being only 0.3% (Table 1). This raises questions about the practical significance of ESC.
    - The reported performance of the baseline SC method is lower than expected. For instance, SC-GPT4 achieves only 60.32% accuracy on MATH, while the official GPT-4 API reports 69.12% accuracy (https://platform.openai.com/docs/models/gpt-4). This discrepancy suggests that the baseline may not have been adequately tuned.
    - The performance of ESC appears to be sensitive to the window size. In Table 2, ESC shows a -2.44% decrease in performance when the window size increases from 8 to 16. This sensitivity raises concerns about the generalizability of ESC.
- The paper lacks a comparison with other efficient variants of self-consistency, such as the one proposed by [1].
- The paper contains several grammatical errors and typos. For example, in Section 1, the phrase should be "based on this" instead of "based on this." In Section 2, "citet" should be used instead of "citep." A thorough proofreading is recommended to enhance the readability.

[1] Yao, Shunyu, et al. "Efficient self-consistency decoding by dynamic early stopping." arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.00600 (2023).

## Questions
- In Section 3.2, the authors mention that "When these $w$ predictions are all the same, the entropy of $P$ is likely to be sufficiently low." Could you elaborate on the reasoning behind this statement? It's not clear why having the same predictions would necessarily imply low entropy.
- In Section 3.2, the authors state that "We will iterate to obtain multiple observation windows until the preset sampling size $L$ is reached if no observation window meets the need during this procedure." Could you clarify what is meant by "no observation window meets the need"? Does this mean that all windows had the same predictions, or what?

The authors address the limitations of prior model merging techniques, which fail when models are trained on disjoint tasks. The proposed method incorporates two strategies: 1) a "zip" operation that allows merging features within each model, and 2) partial zipping up to a specified layer, creating a multi-head model. weaknesses.issue:

review.summary: This paper presents a method for merging two models trained from different tasks that have different initializations. The method combines the concept of permutation (from Git Re-Basin) with feature matching and merging within models. The authors evaluate their method on various different tasks and compare it to baselines.

weaknesses.issue:
1. The authors claim that their method is a generalization of Git Re-Basin for merging models trained on different tasks, but in practice, the method seems to be a specific case of REPAIR. In the “zip” operation, the weights of two models are merged using a feature matching approach similar to REPAIR. The authors don’t consider the effect of batch norm layers, but REPAIR deals with this by adding additional batch norm layers. The “partial zip” operation is essentially similar to REPAIR where some layers are left unmerged. The authors should better explain how their approach generalizes REPAIR rather than the other way around.

2. The authors don’t provide a comparison to REPAIR in any of the experiments. While I agree with the authors that REPAIR adds extra parameters to the model, the authors should either modify REPAIR to allow for partial zipping or the authors should modify their method to allow for additional parameters, and then compare the two approaches. The authors should also compare to Weight Averaging.

3. The experimental results are a bit confusing. In Table 1, why is the ensemble accuracy for CIFAR-100 (50+50) 75%? Shouldn’t it be 100%? In Table 3, why is the ensemble accuracy for ImageNet-1k (200+200) 25%? Shouldn’t it be 100%? Also, in Table 3, why is the Git Re-Basin accuracy 3.1%? In the Git Re-Basin paper, the accuracy is reported to be 20.5%.

The authors show that the measurement scale of the observed variables can affect the performance of such algorithms and that it is possible for a wrong DAG to have minimal score under these assumptions. weaknesses.issue: I am concerned about the novelty and significance of the results. To the best of my knowledge, the results are not novel and have been discussed in earlier works. It is well-known that least squares estimators are inconsistent and it is clear that the measurement scale of the variables affects the optimization landscape of score-based structure learning algorithms, which are minimizing a least squares loss. review.summary: The authors consider the problem of learning the structure of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) from observational data. They focus on score-based algorithms that minimize a loss function (such as MSE or log-likelihood) over the space of DAGs. They show that the optimal solution may change depending on the scale of the variables and that, depending on the relative scales of the variables, the algorithm may converge to a graph with a different structure (e.g. a chain instead of a collider). They also show that this problem persists for more complex structures and non-linear relations between variables. They validate their theoretical results with an empirical study.

weaknesses.issue:
1) The authors assume that the DAG has a very specific structure (chain, fork or collider) and that it has a relatively small number of nodes (up to 10). They also assume that the relations between the variables are linear or of the form $f(X = Pa_X) + \epsilon$. It is not clear whether the observed effects would still be present for larger graphs and more general models.

2) It is also not clear how the results extend to score-based algorithms that use regularization, such as the l1-regularized version of NOTEARS.

3) I think that the contribution of the paper is relatively marginal. The main result is not very surprising and it is limited to very simple settings.

Minor comments:

- I believe that the definition of the MSE should be $||X - f||_2^2$ instead of $||X - f||_F^2$ (the Frobenius norm).

- In the abstract, the authors write "we also show that scale can impair the performance of structure learners for both square based and log-likelihood based losses in non-linear systems". I think the word "impair" is too strong here since it can be seen as a consequence of the previous point.

review.summary: This paper points out the expressive bottleneck of the existing diffusion models. The Gaussian parameterization of the reverse process in the existing diffusion models is not expressive enough to fit the posterior probability, which is possibly multimodal. To solve this problem, the paper proposes soft mixture denoising (SMD). SMD reparameterizes the posterior $p(x_{t-1}|x_t)$ as a mixture of Gaussians where the number of components is infinity. To efficiently control the number of components, SMD introduces a latent variable $z_t$ and reparameterizes the posterior as $p(x_{t-1}|x_t, z_t) = \mathcal{N}(…, z_t)$. In this way, $z_t$ can control the expressiveness of the posterior. The paper proves that SMD has zero local and global denoising errors when $p(x_{t-1}|x_t, z_t)$ is properly parameterized. It also proposes an efficient optimization and sampling method for SMD. Experiments show that SMD consistently improves DDPM, DDIM, ADM, and LDM on CIFAR-10, LSUN-Conference, LSUN-Church, CelebA-HQ, and FFHQ, in terms of FID.

weaknesses.issue:
1. Theorem 1 and Theorem 2 are not rigorous. They do not provide sufficient and necessary conditions for the denoising errors to be unbounded. For example, the paper proves that there exists a data distribution such that the denoising error is unbounded. However, it does not prove that all data distributions will result in an unbounded denoising error. In addition, they do not provide sufficient insights to explain why the existing diffusion models perform well in practice. The denoising error is unbounded only when the denoising steps are small. However, the denoising steps are usually large in practice.

2. The paper does not provide an analysis of the complexity of SMD. The exact number of modes of the posterior is unclear. It is also unclear how the number of modes will affect the complexity. It is unclear how the expressiveness of SMD is related to the number of parameters.

3. The paper does not provide an analysis of the convergence of the training algorithm. The paper needs to provide more details on the training algorithm. For example, how to sample $\eta$, how to sample $z_t$, and how to update $\theta$.

4. The paper does not provide an analysis of the effect of $K$. The exact number of modes of the posterior is unclear. It is unclear how the number of modes will affect the performance.
